paper.title: Establishment of a Three-Dimensional In Vitro Model of Taste Bud Cells for Fat Taste Investigation.
paper.abstract: Fat taste is emerging as a sixth primary taste modality, with CD36 identified as a key receptor for oral detection of long-chain fatty acids. Tastants bind to receptors on taste bud cells (TBCs), triggering intracellular calcium mobilization, neurotransmitter release, activation of gustatory afferent fibers, and transmission of sensory information to the brain. Conventional two-dimensional (2D) culture systems fail to reproduce the complex three-dimensional (3D) architecture and cell-to-cell interactions essential in vivo. Here, we developed a 3D model of mouse TBCs to investigate the cellular mechanisms underlying fat taste perception. Immortalized CD36-positive TBCs and circumvallate papilla-derived TBCs were co-cultured under 2D and 3D conditions. In 3D conditions, TBCs self-organized into spheroids displaying organelles, intercellular junctions, and expression of markers of the three major TBC types. Compared to 2D-cultured cells, spheroids exhibited higher expression of taste receptors, including CD36, sweet receptor T1R2, umami receptor T1R1. Wnt/β-catenin and Sonic Hedgehog pathways, controlling differentiation, were upregulated. Spheroids showed enhanced responses to linoleic acid, with greater intracellular calcium mobilization and serotonin release. This model recapitulates more faithfully structural and functional properties of native taste tissue, providing a physiologically relevant in vitro platform for studies of fat taste mechanisms and potential factors modulating TBC function.

paper.title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists in Dentistry: Promise, Pitfalls, and Evidence Gaps.
paper.abstract: GLP-1RAs (glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists) have become one of the fastest-growing drug classes worldwide, with prescriptions for obesity treatment increasing by 587% from 2019 to 2024. While their metabolic and cardiovascular benefits are well established, the implications for oral health remain largely unexamined. Preclinical evidence consistently demonstrates anti-inflammatory and osteoprotective effects on periodontal and peri-implant tissues: GLP-1RAs promote osteogenic differentiation of periodontal ligament stem cells, reduce alveolar bone resorption in animal models of periodontitis, and enhance implant osseointegration in diabetic rats. However, these findings are based exclusively on in vitro and animal studies, with only a single retrospective cohort study providing limited clinical data. Conversely, several oral adverse effects have been reported based on pharmacovigilance analyses, including xerostomia, dysgeusia, and anosmia, particularly for semaglutide. Gastrointestinal side effects, particularly nausea (15% to 50%), vomiting (5% to 24%), and gastroesophageal reflux, pose a plausible but unquantified risk for tooth erosion and secondary caries. A bidirectional link between GLP-1 signaling and the oral microbiota, mediated by bacterial dipeptidyl peptidase (DPP)-4-like enzymes that degrade endogenous GLP-1, adds further complexity. Despite this breadth of potential interactions, no prospective study has used any dental outcome as an endpoint in patients receiving GLP-1RAs. This critical appraisal synthesizes the evidence across multiple dental disciplines, grades it in each domain, and identifies the gaps that demand urgent investigation.

paper.title: From Food Structure to L-Cell Exposure: How Processing and Digestion Shape Endogenous GLP-1 Responses.
paper.abstract: Interest in using foods to stimulate endogenous glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) has outpaced evidence that transient postprandial increases translate into meaningful physiological outcomes. This review critically examines how food processing and matrix architecture interact with digestion and microbial metabolism to determine the identity, timing, intestinal location, and epithelial accessibility of GLP-1-stimulating ligands. PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science Core Collection, BIOSIS Citation Index, and Scopus were searched for the relevant literature. Evidence from cellular systems, organoids, perfused intestines, animal models, and human studies indicates that sugars, amino acids, peptides, fatty acids, monoacylglycerols, bile acids, and microbial metabolites engage distinct nutrient-sensing pathways. However, GLP-1 responses depend not only on chemical composition but also on cellular integrity, particle size, viscosity, starch organization, emulsion structure, protein processing, fermentation, gastric emptying, and the site of intestinal release. These factors can modify the magnitude and kinetics of GLP-1 exposure, although effects vary considerably with material, dose, comparator, population, and experimental model. Whey-containing preloads provide the most consistent acute human evidence, whereas findings for fibres, emulsions, phytochemicals, fermented foods, and controlled-release approaches remain heterogeneous. Importantly, increases in circulating GLP-1 do not consistently coincide with reduced appetite or energy intake, improved glycaemia, or sustained changes in body weight. Food-induced GLP-1 secretion, reduced degradation through dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibition, and direct GLP-1 receptor agonism therefore represent distinct biological mechanisms. Overall, food structure can modestly and context-dependently modulate endogenous GLP-1 exposure, but current evidence does not support physiological or therapeutic equivalence with pharmacological GLP-1 receptor agonists.

paper.title: Olfactory Swab-Derived Human Neuroepithelium Cell Culture as a Novel Model to Study Neurodegeneration-Related Proteins.
paper.abstract: The olfactory neuroepithelium (ON) collected with nasal swabs (NS) is a valuable source for studying brain processes in physiological and pathological conditions, due to its anatomical proximity to the brain and heterogeneous neural cell population. In this proof-of-concept study, we developed a protocol for co-culturing distinct cellular populations from ON, establishing a human olfactory neuroepithelium cell culture (hON) model from healthy individuals (HIs) without differentiation factors. We characterized the cellular composition of ON samples at harvesting, identifying sustentacular cells (Pan-CK+), neuronal cells (PGP9.5+), and ciliated respiratory cells (βIV-tubulin+) by immunofluorescence and flow cytometry. We assessed the expression and distribution of TDP-43, Tau, and α-synuclein, together with their phosphorylated isoforms, to establish a physiological reference profile. Furthermore, Seeding Amplification Assay (SAA) analysis, including disease-positive and healthy control cohorts, confirmed the absence of aggregated protein species in HIs. While p-Tau and p-α-syn localization was preserved between collection and culture, p-TDP-43 displayed neuron-specific nuclear redistribution upon culture, suggesting distinct regulatory dynamics. Longitudinal monitoring revealed that hON cultures maintain a stable neuronal population for up to 21 days, after which cells transition toward a fibroblast-like phenotype. This study establishes NS-derived hON as a feasible model for investigating neurodegenerative mechanisms, providing a baseline for disease comparisons.

paper.title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists, Gut Microbiota, and Chronic Pain: Nutritional Signaling at the Gut-Brain Axis.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Chronic pain affects more than one in five adults worldwide and is increasingly conceptualized as a disorder of the gut-brain axis. Gut microbial dysbiosis, characterized by reduced alpha-diversity and depletion of short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-producing taxa such as Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Lachnospiraceae, and Roseburia, has been mechanistically linked to pain sensitization. Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), a nutrient-sensing enteroendocrine hormone, and its pharmacological receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) both reshape the gut microbiota and modulate pain across multiple phenotypes. This review synthesizes preclinical and clinical evidence positioning the gut microbiota as a proposed nutritional intermediary that links GLP-1RA pharmacology to chronic pain modulation.

METHODS: We conducted a narrative synthesis of studies retrieved from PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science from inception through 30 June 2026, spanning GLP-1 nutrient sensing, gut microbial alterations in pain, GLP-1RA effects on the microbiome, microbiota-dependent mechanisms, and clinical pain outcomes.

RESULTS: GLP-1 is secreted by L-cells in response to nutrients and microbial SCFAs, signaling to the brain through vagal and humoral routes. GLP-1RAs enrich the same anti-inflammatory, SCFA-producing taxa that are depleted in chronic pain, and their anti-inflammatory actions require an intact microbiota. Mechanistically, GLP-1RAs suppress pain through spinal microglial GLP-1 receptor (GLP-1R)/interleukin-10/beta-endorphin signaling, Nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain (NOD)-, Leucine-rich repeat (LRR)-, and pyrin domain-containing protein 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome inhibition, and receptor-independent transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) blockade, largely independent of glycemic control or weight loss. Clinically, evidence is strongest for knee osteoarthritis and idiopathic intracranial hypertension headache, with emerging signals in fibromyalgia, visceral pain, and reduced opioid use.

CONCLUSIONS: The gut microbiota is proposed to act as both a therapeutic target and a mechanistic intermediary in GLP-1RA-mediated analgesia, a model that awaits direct confirmation in humans. Pain-specific trials incorporating dietary and microbiome endpoints are needed.

paper.title: Nutrient-specific combinatorial secretion of GLP-1 and neurotransmitters in the enteroendocrine L-cell line GLUTag.
paper.abstract: Enteroendocrine L cells function as chemosensors in the intestine, secreting glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) to signal nutrient ingestion to the brain. Since GLP-1 secretion is induced by a variety of nutrients, including sugars, amino acids, and fatty acids, GLP-1 receptor-expressing neurons are also activated regardless of the nutrient identity, making it unclear how the brain discriminates between different nutrients. By examining vesicle dynamics and extracellular signals associated with GLP-1, glutamate, and ATP in GLUTag cells using total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy, a technique that selectively visualizes fluorescent molecules near the plasma membrane, we demonstrated that distinct nutrients evoke specific secretory patterns. D-glucose induced the co-secretion of GLP-1, glutamate, and ATP, whereas L-glutamine induced the secretion of GLP-1 and glutamate but not ATP. Butyrate and sucralose, which are also GLP-1 secretagogues, did not induce the secretion of glutamate or ATP. While Ca2+ acts as the trigger for exocytosis, additional regulatory mechanisms are required to generate these distinct secretory patterns. We therefore investigated the cAMP and cGMP pathways and found that neither their activation nor inhibition detectably affected glutamate and ATP secretion, suggesting the involvement of other nutrient-specific signaling pathways. Collectively, our findings suggest that L cells distinguish and encode nutrient identity as combinatorial secretion patterns of GLP-1 and neurotransmitters.

paper.title: From respiratory viral infection to persistent cough hypersensitivity: neuroimmune regulation and therapeutic implications of P2X3/TRP ion-channel targets.
paper.abstract: Respiratory viral infections are increasingly recognized as important drivers of persistent airway symptoms and exacerbations in chronic lung disease. Post-infectious cough (PIC), particularly after upper respiratory tract infection, represents one of the most frequent causes of subacute cough and a mechanistically complex sequela in which cough hypersensitivity syndrome (CHS) plays a central pathophysiological role. Beyond increased cough frequency, patients with PIC frequently exhibit laryngeal sensory abnormalities and exaggerated responses to low-intensity stimuli, suggesting a sustained reduction in the activation threshold of airway sensory nerves. Among several contributors to cough hypersensitivity, P2X3 receptors and transient receptor potential (TRP) channels are key ion-channel targets mediating cough reflexes and sensory nerve hypersensitivity, yet their clinical translation has been heterogeneous. Gefapixant reduced objective cough frequency in phase III trials enrolling refractory or unexplained chronic cough populations, but these data provide indirect rather than PIC-specific evidence, and its clinical utility is limited by dysgeusia. Similarly, TRPV1 antagonists suppress capsaicin-provoked cough but have not consistently improved spontaneous cough frequency, highlighting a disconnect between provocation models and real-world post-infectious cough pathology. This review discusses how respiratory viruses may induce cough hypersensitivity through transcriptional, metabolic, and neuroimmune regulation of sensory pathways. Respiratory syncytial virus, rhinovirus, and other viral pathogens can upregulate TRPV1, TRPA1, and ASIC3 expression, while cytokines such as IFN-γ may promote sensory-neuron transcriptional reprogramming through JAK-STAT and NF-κB signaling. In parallel, inflammatory mediators including bradykinin, COX/12-LOX metabolites, and prostaglandin E2 can sensitize TRP channels through kinase-dependent phosphorylation, whereas virus-induced epithelial ATP release and impaired CD39/CD73-mediated purinergic degradation may sustain repeated P2X3 receptor activation. Persistent peripheral afferent input may further induce central sensitization, explaining residual cough despite peripheral target blockade. By integrating viral immunopathogenesis, epithelial-neural crosstalk, and ion-channel pharmacology, this review proposes a framework for understanding post-viral cough hypersensitivity as a neuroimmune sequela of respiratory infection. Future research should prioritize molecular endotype-based stratification, PIC-specific randomized controlled trials, optimization of highly selective P2X3 antagonists, and combined peripheral-central assessment strategies to guide more precise therapeutic interventions.

paper.title: Olfactory ensheathing cell-derived extracellular vesicles protect the degenerated retinal pigment epithelium by delivering phagocytosis-related proteins.
paper.abstract: Aim: Olfactory ensheathing cells (OECs) are commonly utilized in cell-based therapies for neurodegenerative diseases and central nervous system injuries, due to their unique properties of suppressing gliosis and providing neuroprotection. Small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) have emerged as promising therapeutic agents. This study aimed to investigate OEC-sEVs' effect on retinal degeneration. Methods: Proteomics analysis identified differentially expressed proteins between OEC-sEVs and OECs. We conducted subretinal injection of OEC-sEVs and assessed their protective mechanisms in degenerative retina. Real-time quantitative PCR and Western blot were used to detect the expression of phagocytosis-related molecules in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells. Results: Proteomics analysis revealed that proteins enriched in OEC-sEVs were associated with phagocytosis. Following injection into the subretinal spaces of Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) rats, OEC-sEVs were internalized by RPE cells, leading to the transient upregulation of tyrosine-protein kinase Mer (MerTK), activation of the downstream phosphoinositide 3-kinase/Akt signaling pathway, and restoration of the phagocytic activity of RPE cells towards the photoreceptor outer segments. This delayed photoreceptor degeneration, thereby improving retinal function in RCS rats. In the ARPE-19 cell line treated with the specific MerTK inhibitor UNC2881, enhanced phagocytosis of fluorescent particles and porcine photoreceptor outer segments was observed following OEC-sEV internalization. Conclusion: OEC-sEVs were abundant in proteins associated with phagocytosis, which may partially compensate for the phagocytic deficit of the RPE cells observed in a retinitis pigmentosa rat model via the MerTK-related signaling pathway.

paper.title: Hydrogen gas and olfactory dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease: the Hydrogen-Olfactory-Limbic hypothesis.
paper.abstract: Olfactory dysfunction is increasingly recognized as an early clinical feature of Alzheimer's disease (AD), often preceding measurable cognitive impairment and associated with subsequent cognitive decline. Despite this relatively consistent clinical association, the anatomical, cellular, and physiological substrates underlying olfactory dysfunction in AD remain poorly understood. Post-mortem human studies have identified amyloid-β (Aβ) and tau pathology in olfactory structures, including the olfactory epithelium and anterior olfactory nucleus. However, the available anatomical evidence remains limited, and the presence of these pathological proteins does not establish that they cause olfactory dysfunction. Likewise, it remains uncertain whether early olfactory impairment reflects peripheral sensory dysfunction, neuronal loss, synaptic or circuit abnormalities, altered higher-order olfactory processing, disruption of olfactory-limbic networks, or a combination of these processes. Although the olfactory epithelium possesses lifelong regenerative capacity, whether this capacity is altered during AD progression remains unresolved. Molecular hydrogen (H₂) has demonstrated antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, mitochondrial-modulatory, and cytoprotective effects in diverse experimental systems. However, direct evidence that hydrogen modifies AD-associated olfactory dysfunction is currently lacking. In this Perspective, we propose the Hydrogen-Olfactory-Limbic hypothesis as an experimentally testable framework rather than an established therapeutic mechanism. We suggest that molecular hydrogen can serve as an experimental intervention to determine whether modulating oxidative, inflammatory, and metabolic processes affects olfactory function and olfactory-limbic circuit physiology during AD progression. This framework integrates behavioral, anatomical, molecular, electrophysiological, regenerative, and connectivity measurements to address two fundamental questions: what causes early olfactory dysfunction in AD, and can molecular hydrogen modify biologically relevant processes associated with this phenotype?

paper.title: Luteolin alleviates neurogenic inflammation in OVA-induced combined allergic rhinitis and asthma syndrome mice through TRPV1/ERK-related signaling.
paper.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Combined Allergic Rhinitis and Asthma Syndrome (CARAS), a common chronic allergic respiratory disease, involves dysregulated neuro-immune interactions and neurogenic inflammation. Luteolin (LUT) has significant anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activities. However, its effects and underlying mechanism in CARAS remain unclear. This study aims to determine the effects of LUT administration during the airway challenge phase of CARAS and its association with TRPV1/ERK signaling.

METHODS: BALB/C mice were used to establish an ovalbumin (OVA)-induced CARAS model and LUT was administered. The nasal symptoms were evaluated by counting the number of nasal scratching and sneezing. HE and toluidine blue staining were performed to determine the histopathological changes. Total and differential cell counts in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) were determined. The levels of histamine, MCP-1, substance P (SP), CGRP and Th1/Th2/Th17-related cytokines were detected by ELISA kit. Besides, TRPV1 and p-ERK expression levels were measured by immunofluorescence staining and Western blotting.

RESULTS: Our study indicated that LUT administration significantly reduced sneezing frequency, nasal scratching behavior, and serum OVA-specific IgE level in CARAS mice compared to the model group. Histopathological analysis demonstrated that LUT administration reduced inflammatory cell accumulation and histological scores in the nasal mucosa and lung tissues and was associated with reduced inflammatory cell counts in BALF. In addition, LUT administration reduced mast cell density in both tissues. Serum histamine and MCP-1 levels and pulmonary levels of IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, IL-17A, and IFN-γ were also reduced following LUT administration. LUT administration also reduced serum and BALF levels of SP and CGRP. Furthermore, LUT administration reduced TRPV1 expression and p-ERK levels in the nasal mucosa and lung tissue.

CONCLUSION: LUT administration attenuates allergic and inflammatory responses in OVA-induced CARAS mice, which may be associated with TRPV1/ERK signaling.

paper.title: Olfactory context and memory across the adult lifespan: effects on mnemonic discrimination and olfactory function.
paper.abstract: Odor is a powerful contextual cue that can influence memory and is closely linked to brain regions involved in episodic memory, including the hippocampus. Age-related olfactory dysfunction is among the earliest behavioral changes associated with cognitive decline and may contribute to memory impairments in older adults. Hippocampal pattern separation, or the process of reducing interference among similar experiences, provides a sensitive measure of age-related memory decline, yet little is known about how olfactory context influences mnemonic discrimination. In the present study, we examined whether odor context during encoding affects subsequent mnemonic discrimination in young and older adults. Participants completed a mnemonic similarity task in which object stimuli were encoded in both odor (lavender) and no-odor contexts prior to a memory test. Across participants, odor context did not significantly influence target recognition or mnemonic discrimination. Consistent with prior work, older adults exhibited poorer mnemonic discrimination and reduced olfactory function relative to young adults. However, odor presentation order influenced mnemonic discrimination in older adults, such that performance was better when the odor context was encountered during the first encoding block compared to the second. Additionally, poorer olfactory function was associated with reduced mnemonic discrimination, and this relationship was largely explained by age-related differences in olfactory ability. These findings suggest that the influence of olfactory context on memory depends on both age and the timing of odor exposure, highlighting the importance of individual differences in olfactory function when evaluating odor-based approaches to support memory in aging.

paper.title: Detection of serotonin and serotonin-related genes reveals unique roles in human intestinal epithelial development.
paper.abstract: Although 95% of serotonin in the human body is produced in the gastrointestinal tract, most prior research work has focused on the brain. Despite its abundance in the gut, serotonin's role in early intestinal development remains poorly understood. Here we show that serotonin is detected in both the small intestine and large intestine as early as 14 to 15 weeks gestational age. Using single-cell transcriptomics with histological validation, we generated a spatiotemporal atlas of serotonin and serotonin-related genes in the human gut from first trimester to late adulthood. The serotonin synthesis gene, TPH1, was exclusively expressed in enteroendocrine cells at all time points analyzed, with the highest expression in the second trimester. The serotonin reuptake gene, SLC6A4, was largely restricted to mature absorptive enterocytes and increased postnatally. Serotonin receptors also displayed distinct cellular and developmental expression patterns. HTR1E was confined to the first trimester during highly proliferative stage. HTR4 was enriched for in crypt regions, suggesting a role in proliferation for serotonin. Finally, HTR3E was associated with tuft cells throughout development. Together, these findings reveal the dynamic, cell-type-specific regulation of serotonin in the developing human gut, suggesting its importance in early intestinal development, and provide a framework to study its roles in intestinal development and diseases.

paper.title: Facial Nerve Palsy With Olfactory and Gustatory Dysfunction Following COVID-19 Infection: An Illustrative Case-Based Narrative Review.
paper.abstract: COVID-19 infection has been recognized to induce a wide range of neurological manifestations, ranging in severity from transient, benign manifestations to severe neurological deficits. Cranial nerve involvement, particularly facial, olfactory, and gustatory nerve dysfunction, has emerged as a notable clinical feature in affected individuals. This review article aims to present and analyze three confirmed COVID-19 diagnoses that exhibited facial nerve palsy (FNP), olfactory disturbances (OD), and/or gustatory disturbances (GD), while also exploring the potential underlying pathophysiological mechanisms of these symptoms. This article presents three cases of laboratory-confirmed COVID-19 in which patients developed FNP along with OD and/or GD, and discusses their potential pathophysiological mechanisms. All three patients had hallmark signs and symptoms of FNP, with dysgeusia present in three and anosmia present in two. COVID-19 was confirmed with reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) testing. Neuroimaging and cerebrospinal fluid analysis ruled out other differential diagnostic possibilities. Treatment strategies varied from case to case and included steroids, antivirals, and traditional medicine. Outcomes ranged from partial to complete recovery of FNP within four weeks. The three presented cases suggest a temporal association between COVID-19 and FNP, though case reports alone cannot establish causation. While direct neural invasion, immune response, or ischemic injury are potential mechanisms, a definitive cause has not yet been established. OD and GD in the presented cases were short-lived, which may suggest, but cannot confirm, a mechanism different from direct cranial nerve involvement. This remains speculative given the small sample size. Further research is warranted to elucidate the pathophysiology of cranial nerve involvement, thereby guiding diagnosis and treatment strategies.

paper.title: Volatile Chemistry and Aroma Differences in Commercial Soy Sauces: Sensory Links and Odorant-Receptor Interactions.
paper.abstract: Volatile and sensory differences among 28 commercial soy sauces were investigated using HS-GC-IMS, check-all-that-apply (CATA) evaluation, aroma addition experiments, and molecular docking. Ninety-nine volatile compounds from 14 chemical classes were detected. Total semiquantitative volatile concentrations ranged from 2024.56 to 6279.59 μg/mL, with esters, alcohols, and aldehydes accounting for 70.68% of the total. Of the 24 CATA descriptors, 13 were retained for product-level correlation analysis. Exploratory Pearson analysis indicated that alcoholic, savory, and malty attributes were associated with a group dominated by fatty acids, branched-chain alcohols, and esters, whereas woody and chocolate-like attributes showed an opposing pattern involving several aldehydes, ketones, and alkylpyrazines. Fifteen candidate compounds were evaluated by single-compound addition. Benzaldehyde and ethyl propanoate enhanced savory perception; 2-ethyl-3,5-dimethylpyrazine enhanced the alcoholic attribute; methyl 2-methylbutyrate enhanced smoky, meaty, and alcoholic attributes; and ethyl acetate enhanced malty, meaty, and alcoholic attributes. Several other additions produced opposing or nonsignificant effects, indicating matrix- and concentration-dependent responses. Among the binary docking models, guaiacol-2-ethyl-3,5-dimethylpyrazine and homofuraneol-benzaldehyde produced the lowest scores with OR10G4 (-10.10 kcal/mol) and OR5M3 (-13.32 kcal/mol), respectively. In combination, these results show that product-level correlations can guide candidate selection but require matrix-based sensory verification, while docking provides structural hypotheses for odorant co-binding.

paper.title: Olfactory dysfunction and limbic volumetric changes in relapsing-remitting and secondary progressive multiple sclerosis.
paper.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To compare olfactory performance and olfactory-related brain region volumes between patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) and secondary progressive multiple sclerosis (SPMS) and to examine the relationship between olfactory performance and regional brain volumes.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: This prospective cross-sectional study included 65 patients with MS (43 RRMS and 22 SPMS). Olfactory function was assessed using the Sniffin' Sticks-12 Odor Identification Test. Bilateral volumes of the hippocampus, amygdala, entorhinal cortex, and insular cortex were obtained from three-dimensional T1-weighted MRI using the vol2Brain automated analysis pipeline available through the volBrain platform. Both raw and total intracranial volume (TIV)-normalized regional volumes were analyzed. For volumetric outcomes, multivariable analyses were adjusted for age, sex, and TIV, whereas analyses of olfactory performance were adjusted for age and sex. Additional sensitivity analyses incorporated disease duration and EDSS.

RESULTS: In unadjusted comparisons, patients with SPMS had significantly lower Sniffin' Sticks-12 scores than those with RRMS (p = 0.004), and raw hippocampal volume was significantly lower in the SPMS group (p = 0.028). However, after adjustment for age, sex, and TIV, clinical subtype was not independently associated with hippocampal, amygdala, entorhinal cortex, or insular cortex volume (all p > 0.05). These findings remained non-significant in sensitivity analyses additionally accounting for disease duration and EDSS. The between-group difference in Sniffin' Sticks-12 scores was also attenuated after adjustment for age and sex (B = - 1.06; 95% CI, - 2.15 to 0.04; p = 0.058) and remained non-significant in further sensitivity analyses. No significant correlations were observed between Sniffin' Sticks-12 scores and regional volumetric measures.

CONCLUSION: Although patients with SPMS showed poorer olfactory performance and lower raw hippocampal volume in unadjusted comparisons, clinical subtype was not independently associated with regional brain volumes after adjustment for age, sex, and TIV, and the olfactory difference did not reach statistical significance after adjustment for age and sex. Furthermore, olfactory performance was not directly associated with regional volumetric measures, suggesting that olfactory dysfunction in MS may reflect mechanisms beyond regional structural volume alone.

paper.title: Sinonasal and Olfactory Quality of Life Following Endonasal Transsphenoidal Surgery for Pituitary Adenoma: A Multicenter Prospective Cohort Triphasic Recovery Analysis in Ethiopia.
paper.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To characterize the sinonasal and olfactory quality of life (QoL) trajectory.

METHODS: A multicenter prospective cohort study was conducted on 91 patients undergoing TSS at Addis Ababa University teaching hospitals between May 2024 and August 2025. QoL was evaluated using the Sino-Nasal Outcome Test (SNOT-22) questionnaire v4 preoperatively and at 3- and 6-month postoperatively.

RESULTS: Analysis revealed a characteristic triphasic recovery pattern: low preoperative baseline, a transient peak in morbidity at 3 months, and an improvement toward baseline by 6 months for most systemic domains. At 3 months, significant score worsening occurred for loss of smell/taste (mean: 1.7, p < 0.001), thick discharge (mean: 1.0, p < 0.001), congestion (mean: 1.0, p < 0.001), postnasal discharge (mean: 0.7, p < 0.001), and runny nose (mean: 0.5, p = 0.003). By 6 months, persistence was confined to loss of smell/taste (p < 0.001), thick discharge (p < 0.001), and congestion (p = 0.005). Exploratory analysis in the nasoseptal flap cohort (n = 3) showed higher scores. Preliminary findings of delayed ear pain/fullness in acromegaly at 6 months hypothesized to reflect a link between growth hormone normalization and altered Eustachian tube function. Poorer sleep with binostril access (p = 0.017) speculatively associated with bilateral synechiae under limited postoperative care. Unlike Western cohorts, protracted recovery may reflect lack of standardized high-volume saline irrigation and scheduled debridement.

CONCLUSIONS: TSS demonstrates a favorable long-term QoL profile; however, localized sinonasal and olfactory deficits often persist at 6 months.

paper.title: Olfactory dysfunction and submicroscopic abnormalities: unveiling hidden pathologies.
paper.abstract: Recent advances in high-resolution genomic technologies have revealed that several syndromes are associated with submicroscopic chromosomal deletions and, less frequently, duplications, thereby substantially contributing to the functional annotation of the human genome. Among these structural variants, recurrent microdeletions or microduplications often disrupt dosage-sensitive genes, leading to shared phenotypic outcomes in affected individuals. While features such as congenital heart defects, neurodevelopmental delays, and intellectual disability (ID) have been extensively studied, phenotypes resulting in olfactory dysfunction remain largely underexplored. Here, we review reported cases of copy number variants (CNVs) in patients with isolated or syndromic olfactory impairment and stratify the strength of associations between CNVs and olfactory dysfunction using predefined evidence levels. The available evidence ranges from well-supported loci with documented human olfactory phenotypes and mechanistic evidence to hypothesis-generating observations based primarily on isolated cases or biological plausibility. By distinguishing these levels of evidence, we highlight both established dosage-sensitive pathways involved in olfactory development and major limitations of the current literature, including incomplete olfactory phenotyping and the difficulty of interpreting large multigenic CNVs. This framework may facilitate more rigorous genotype-phenotype interpretation in congenital and syndromic olfactory disorders.

paper.title: Comparing two case definitions for including severe acute respiratory infection patients in influenza and COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness studies among older adults using the test-negative design: VEBIS hospital network, seven European countries, 2023/24.
paper.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Two severe acute respiratory infection (SARI) case definitions (CDs) are often used in test-negative design (TND) hospital-based vaccine effectiveness (VE) studies. SARI-CD1 requires ≥1 symptom (cough, fever, shortness of breath, anosmia, ageusia, or dysgeusia); SARI-CD2 requires both fever and cough. Using VEBIS hospital network end-of-season 2023/24 data, we compared the effect of these CDs on influenza and COVID-19 VE estimates in Europe.

METHODS: Using the TND, we restricted analysis to seven countries recruiting patients using SARI-CD1; we created a subset of SARI patients also meeting SARI-CD2. Cases were RT-PCR-positive for influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), or SARS-CoV-2; controls were influenza or SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR-negative. We estimated VE among patients ≥65 years using logistic regression adjusted for country, onset date, age, sex, and chronic conditions. We estimated VE overall, by age group (65-79, ≥80 years) and time since vaccination (14-59, 60-119, ≥120 days). Absolute VE differences ≥10% were considered relevant.

RESULTS: Patient characteristics and outcomes were similar across CDs. SARI-CD1 had slightly more vaccinated cases, with little difference in controls between the two CDs. For influenza, the absolute VE difference between SARI-CD1 and SARI-CD2 was 10% for influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 (34% vs 44%), 19% among those aged ≥80 years (21% vs 40%) and 18% at 60-119 days post-vaccination (4% vs 22%). For SARS-CoV-2, absolute VE differences were 11% overall (29% vs 40%), 11% among ≥80 years (33% vs 44%), and 12% at 60-119 days (34% vs 46%). All other absolute VE differences were < 10%.

CONCLUSIONS: VE was similar for influenza A(H3N2), adults 65-79 years and 14-60 days post-vaccination. We observed signals of higher VE with SARI-CD2 for influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 and SARS-CoV-2, particularly among adults ≥80 years and ≥ 60 days post-vaccination, although 95% CIs overlapped. These signals suggest CDs may contribute to VE variability and VE studies should clearly indicate CDs used.

paper.title: Auditory-Olfactory Integration in Simulated Natural Environments Dissociates Neural and Subjective Responses in Visually Impaired Individuals.
paper.abstract: Visually impaired individuals rely on cross-modal plasticity to compensate for absent visual input, yet the neurophysiological mechanisms underlying naturalistic auditory-olfactory integration remain poorly characterized. This study investigated how combined auditory and olfactory cues in representative landscape scenarios modulate cortical activity and multidimensional perceptual experience in 20 visually impaired participants. Five ecologically distinct scenarios-wooded resting areas, dynamic water features, aromatic planting beds, open lawns, and hard-paved plazas-were simulated using synchronized playback of field-recorded soundscapes and calibrated odor diffusion systems. Participants completed standardized ratings across auditory, olfactory, and integrated perceptual dimensions while electroencephalographic (EEG) recordings were acquired. Occipital α/β ratios (O1/O2) served as the primary neurophysiological index of cortical relaxation. Results demonstrated a dissociation between explicit hedonic appraisal and implicit neurophysiological response: dynamic water soundscapes dominated subjective preference ratings, whereas floral olfactory cues in low-amplitude acoustic contexts elicited the highest α/β ratios, significantly exceeding those recorded in wooded and open lawn scenarios. Odor familiarity correlated inversely with α/β elevation (r = -0.46, p < 0.05), indicating that unfamiliar floral scents triggered more robust relaxation responses than familiar urban olfactory environments. This correlation may reflect novelty-related attentional processes rather than relaxation per se. Exploratory clustering revealed stable, trait-like individual differences in baseline α/β activity that were not explained by perceptual ratings, and linear mixed-effects modeling confirmed that inter-individual baseline differences, rather than linear coupling with conscious evaluations, drove α/β variance. Given the relatively small sample size, these findings should be regarded as preliminary and hypothesis-generating. Nevertheless, they extend current models of cross-modal neuroplasticity by demonstrating that naturalistic multisensory integration follows dissociable subjective and neurophysiological trajectories, informing evidence-based multisensory interventions for accessible environmental design.

paper.title: Cognitive assessment of patients with post-COVID olfactory dysfunction and impaired domains.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Persistent olfactory dysfunction is a common symptom of post-COVID syndrome (PCS), particularly among younger patients who experienced mild COVID-19. Recent functional neuroimaging studies suggest that persistent olfactory impairment may be associated with cognitive deficits. However, few studies have characterised cognition in this subgroup using standardised neuropsychological assessment.

OBJECTIVES: To assess the prevalence of cognitive deficits and their characteristics in patients with persistent post-COVID olfactory symptoms.

METHODS: This multicentre study included 55 patients with PCS and persistent olfactory dysfunction following COVID-19 onset before February 2021. Participants underwent olfactory evaluation using the Sniffin' Sticks test and a comprehensive battery of neuropsychological assessments.

RESULTS: The mean age was 43.9 years (SD 10.1), with a mean disease duration of 46.1 months (SD 6.5). According to a domain-based criterion, 67.3% of patients showed cognitive impairment. Domain-specific impairment was observed in attention/working memory (67.3%), executive function (50.9%), and episodic memory (56.4%). The Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) detected abnormalities in only 9.1% of patients. Exploratory comparisons between hyposmic and anosmic patients showed no univariate differences after false discovery rate (FDR) correction, despite a marginal post-hoc multivariate effect. Continuous olfactory performance showed inverse correlations with two executive measures after FDR correction, but no consistent dose-response relationship across cognitive measures.

CONCLUSION: In this selected cohort, a high prevalence of multidomain cognitive alterations was observed. These findings highlight the limitations of brief cognitive screening tools and suggest a complex relationship between persistent olfactory dysfunction and cognition. Further longitudinal studies are warranted.

paper.title: Herpes simplex virus, APOE ε4, and olfactory function in older adults: A cohort study.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Olfactory dysfunction (OD) is associated with neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer's disease (AD). Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV1) may increase AD risk, but longitudinal changes in olfaction related to HSV1 carriage and apolipoprotein ε4 (APOE ε4) status remain unclear.

OBJECTIVE: To investigate if OD is associated with carriage of HSV1, and whether APOE ε4 status modulates this possible association.

METHODS: From a large population-based cohort study in northern Sweden (Betula study), 1288 individuals with a baseline odor identification assessment were included, with follow-up assessment (n = 950) after five or ten years. Odor sensitivity (odor threshold test) was tested at a single time point for 651 individuals. HSV1 carriership and apolipoprotein E genotype were established for all participants.

RESULTS: Weighted linear mixed-model analyses showed that carriage of HSV1, regardless of APOE ε4 status, was not associated with decline in odor identification. At baseline, male gender and higher age were associated with impaired odor identification, while better semantic memory was associated with better odor identification ability. Higher age, low education level and better semantic memory were associated with poorer odor identification performance over time. Furthermore, multiple linear regression showed that male gender, higher age and low education level were significantly associated with impaired odor sensitivity.

CONCLUSIONS: HSV1 did not associate with OD in this population-based cohort study with 5-10 years of follow-up, where olfaction was measured and analyzed using two different objective measurements. The association between OD and neurodegenerative diseases needs further investigation.

paper.title: Case Report: Olfactory loss as the sentinel manifestation of type 2 chronic rhinosinusitis without polyps: response to IL-4Rα inhibition with stapokibart - a case series.
paper.abstract: Chronic rhinosinusitis without nasal polyps (CRSsNP) is traditionally associated with type 1 inflammation, but emerging evidence reveals a subset of patients with a type 2 endotype driven by IL-4 and IL-13, often presenting with prominent olfactory dysfunction and responding poorly to conventional therapy. All had elevated type 2 biomarkers, absence of nasal polyps, and CT evidence of sinusitis. After failure of intranasal corticosteroids, they received stapokibart (600 mg loading dose, then 300 mg every two weeks for 16 weeks). Olfactory improvement occurred within two weeks and was sustained through week 16; SNOT-22 scores decreased by approximately 90%, and Lund-Mackay scores decreased to 0 (Cases 1 and 2) and 1 (Case 3). Serum total IgE decreased in all patients; eosinophil counts decreased in two but paradoxically increased in one. No serious adverse events occurred. Type 2 CRSsNP with prominent olfactory dysfunction is a distinct, treatable phenotype. Stapokibart rapidly improves olfactory function in patients refractory to conventional therapy, supporting an endotype-driven biologic strategy for CRS.

paper.title: Prospective study comparing olfactory function in patients undergoing nasoseptal and rescue flap.

OBJECTIVE: Endoscopic skull base surgery, whether for treatment or reconstruction, can affect olfaction. Assessing whether the rescue flap technique leads to better olfactory recovery than the nasoseptal flap is essential for developing criteria to guide surgical flap selection. paper.title: Environmental Exposures, Chronic Sinusitis, and Olfaction in People With Cystic Fibrosis.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Environmental air pollutants may contribute to chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS), but their relationship with upper airway disease in people with cystic fibrosis (CF) remains poorly understood. This study evaluated associations between long-term ambient air pollutant exposure and CRS severity and olfactory dysfunction in adults with CF and CRS.

METHODS: 80 adults with CF and comorbid CRS were prospectively enrolled from 2019 to 2023 at multiple U.S. academic rhinology centers. Long-term exposure to PM2.5, PM10, CO, SO2, NO2, and ozone was estimated using the nearest U.S. Environmental Protection Agency monitor linked to each participant's residential ZIP code, with 3-year mean exposure calculated before enrollment. CRS severity and olfaction were assessed using Lund-Kennedy endoscopy scores, Lund-Mackay CT scores, SNOT-22, Questionnaire of Olfactory Disorders-Negative Statements, and 40-item Smell Identification Test. Analyses used Spearman correlations and nonparametric group comparisons.

RESULTS: Higher ozone exposure was associated with worse total SNOT-22 scores (Rs = 0.34 p = 0.002), including ear/facial, psychological, and sleep dysfunction domains, as well as worse olfactory-specific outcomes, including higher QOD-NS scores (Rs = 0.30, p = 0.007) and lower Smell Identification Test scores (Rs = -0.30, p = 0.018). Other pollutants did not show significant associations with CRS or olfactory outcomes.

CONCLUSIONS: In adults with CF and CRS, higher long-term ambient ozone exposure was associated with greater sinonasal symptom burden and worse olfactory function. These findings suggest that ozone may be an environmental contributor to upper airway disease severity in this population and support further study in larger, adjusted analyses.

KEY POINTS: Increased ozone pollution correlates with more severe CRS in people with CF. Among people with CF and CRS, higher ozone exposure is associated with worse olfactory function.

paper.title: A Cross-Sectional Study of Patient Views on Acceptability of Olfactory Implants.
paper.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Unlike other chronic conditions, effective therapies for smell and taste disorders (SATDs) remain scarce. Olfactory implants are an emerging area of therapy aimed at restoring the sense of smell through electrical stimulation of the olfactory pathway. This survey aimed to assess patient opinions and the acceptability of olfactory implants, including willingness to undergo surgery, as well as factors influencing their decision-making process.

DESIGN AND SETTING: This was a cross-sectional survey consisting of two online questionnaires circulated via the charity SmellTaste, exploring features and impacts of SATDs, and opinions surrounding olfactory implants in those formally diagnosed or self-identifying with SATDs.

RESULTS: A total of 410 participants completed the primary questionnaire assessing general demographics and olfactory experiences. A further 47 participants completed the second, more in-depth questionnaire about the perceptions on olfactory implants. Across both questionnaires, more females responded than males-a trend seen throughout research on SATDs. An overwhelming majority of participants would be willing to wear a non-implantable device to help detect odour quantity and quality, especially if used to detect dangers such as gas and fires. Opinions on surgically implantable devices varied more. Most patients were amenable prior to any mention of risks, but further probing revealed understanding risks and success rates of any procedure were key to guiding patient decisions.

CONCLUSION: There are patients with olfactory loss who are willing to use an olfactory implant; therefore, more extensive research into the safety, viability and efficacy of olfactory implants is needed.

paper.title: Synaptic connectome of a neurosecretory network in the Drosophila brain.
paper.abstract: Hormones mediate inter-organ signaling, which is crucial in orchestrating diverse behaviors and physiological processes, including sleep and activity, feeding, growth, metabolism, and reproduction. The pars intercerebralis and pars lateralis in insects represent major hubs that contain neurosecretory cells (NSCs) that produce various peptide hormones. To obtain insight into how hormonal signaling is regulated, we have characterized the synaptic connectome of NSCs in the adult Drosophila brain. Identification of neurons providing inputs to multiple NSC classes implicates diuretic hormone 44-expressing NSCs as a major coordinator of physiology and behavior. Surprisingly, despite most NSCs having dendrites in the subesophageal zone (primary taste processing center), inputs from peripheral gustatory neurons to NSCs are largely indirect. We also deciphered pathways via which diverse olfactory inputs are relayed to NSCs. Using an influence metric, based on a linear dynamical systems approach, we identify enteric neurons as the strongest influencers of NSC activity compared to other sensory modalities. Further, our analyses revealed substantial inputs from brain descending neurons to NSCs, suggesting that descending neurons regulate both endocrine and motor output to synchronize physiological changes with appropriate behaviors. In contrast to NSC inputs, synaptic output from NSCs is sparse and mostly mediated by corazonin NSCs. We show that both corazonin-expressing NSCs and their downstream synaptic partner DNg27 influence egg-laying. We additionally explore putative paracrine interconnectivity between NSC classes and peptide hormone pathways from NSCs to peripheral tissues by analyzing single-cell transcriptomic datasets. Our comprehensive characterization of the Drosophila neurosecretory network connectome provides a platform to understand complex hormonal networks and how they orchestrate animal behaviors and physiology.

paper.title: MaltEms-MaltOBP9 axis mediates sexually dimorphic olfactory behavior in Monochamus alternatus via recognition of pheromone 2-methoxy-4-vinylphenol.

These findings provide a theoretical basis for developing pest control methods that target MaltOBP9 and its critical residue Phe54 through behavior-based strategies.

paper.title: Transcranial Photobiomodulation Attenuates Neurogenic Inflammation and Sensory Hypersensitivity in a Nitroglycerin-Induced Migraine Model: Toward a Nonpharmacological Therapy.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Migraine is a debilitating neurological condition, characterized by headache, photophobia, and heightened mechanical/thermal sensitivity. Current pharmacological therapies often lead to incomplete relief and adverse effects, necessitating the use of noninvasive alternatives. This study evaluated transcranial photobiomodulation (PBM) in a nitroglycerin (NTG)-induced migraine model in male mice.

METHODS: Mice were assigned to Sham, NTG, NTG + Sumatriptan (SUMA; 600 µg/kg, s.c.), NTG + PBM, and NTG + PBM + SUMA groups. Over 9 days, NTG (5 mg/kg) was injected intraperitoneally every other day to develop an animal model of chronic migraine. The PBM protocol involved daily irradiation (810 nm) on the occipital bone of the head for 5 s over 9 days. The animals underwent behavioral testing for photophobia, mechanical allodynia, and thermal sensitivity. The trigeminal nucleus caudalis (TNC) was assessed for miR-155 expression by real-time PCR and protein expression of phospho-NF-κB, IL-1β, transient receptor potential ankyrin 1 (TRPA1) and vanilloid 1 (TRPV1), calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), c-Fos, and pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP) using immunoblotting.

RESULTS: Behavioral assessment revealed that PBM significantly reduced head scratching and improved exploratory activity, decreased light aversion, reversed periorbital/hindpaw mechanical allodynia, and prolonged thermal withdrawal latency compared to the NTG group. Moreover, PBM downregulated miR-155 expression and decreased levels of inflammatory mediators and migraine-associated neuropeptides in the TNC. Notably, combined PBM and SUMA treatment resulted in improvements in behavioral and molecular outcomes compared to either treatment alone.

CONCLUSION: These results indicate that PBM inhibited migraine-like behaviors and decreased the expression of numerous molecular markers that are linked to neuroinflammation and trigeminal activation in the TNC. These findings establish a foundation for additional research on transcranial PBM as a noninvasive method for modulating migraine-related behavioral responses.

paper.title: The effects of olfactory stimulation on postural control in adults: A systematic review.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Olfactory stimulation has emerged as a potential modulator of postural control, yet the evidence has not been systematically synthesized. This systematic review aimed to aggregate, critically appraise, and narratively synthesize the available literature on the effects of olfactory stimulation on postural control in adults.

METHODS: This systematic review was conducted according to the PRISMA 2020 guideline and the Cochrane Handbook. The protocol was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261326528). A systematic search of PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus was performed from inception to December 1, 2025, supplemented by grey literature searches and reference list screening. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-experimental designs, and clinical trials examining olfactory stimulation effects on any quantitative measure of postural control were eligible. Two reviewers independently performed study selection, data extraction, and quality assessment using the Downs and Black checklist. The certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) framework. Due to substantial methodological and clinical heterogeneity, a narrative synthesis was conducted following the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) guidelines.

RESULTS: Ten studies (six RCTs and four Non-RCTs) involving 365 participants (mean age 47.9 ± 19.8 years) were included. Olfactory stimulation with pleasant odors (e.g., lavender, black pepper) generally enhanced postural stability, particularly in older adults and under eyes-closed conditions, while unpleasant odors consistently increased postural sway. However, inhibitory effects were observed during high-precision athletic tasks. Odor-specific effects were identified, with appetitive cues producing unique facilitatory effects. According to GRADE, the certainty of evidence was moderate for dynamic balance and functional mobility, low for fear of falling, and very low for static balance.

CONCLUSION: Olfactory stimulation can modulate postural control in adults, with effects dependent on odor valence, participant traits, and task demands. Pleasant odors generally enhance stability during sensory deprivation, while unpleasant odors increase sway; however, trigeminal stimulants like ammonia may impair high-precision tasks. Evidence certainty was low to moderate, warranting cautious interpretation. These findings lay the groundwork for future research on olfactory-motor integration and clinical applications in balance rehabilitation and fall prevention. Registration: The study was registered on the International Prospective Registry of Systematic Reviews database (CRD420261326528).

paper.title: "Health Is in the Air": Visual and Olfactory Nudges and Food Choices at University Vending Machines.
paper.abstract: Background/Objectives: Ambient sensory cues can influence food choice, yet their role in everyday environments remains underexplored, with much of the existing evidence derived from laboratory studies. This is particularly relevant in university settings, where students often make rapid, convenience-driven choices that may be nudged toward healthier options by sensory cues (e.g., images or scents). Methods: A quasi-experimental field study was conducted across three consecutive one-week conditions: control, visual (a nature-themed poster), and olfactory (jasmine fragrance). Snacks were classified according to perceived healthiness ratings from a pre-study questionnaire. After predefined exclusions, purchases were analyzed using binary logistic regression, with condition as the main predictor and price and time of day examined as additional factors. Results: Among N = 1043 purchases, products classified as healthy were more frequent during the olfactory week than during the control and visual weeks. The visual condition did not differ significantly from control. Higher prices were associated with lower odds of purchasing a product classified as healthy, whereas time of day was not significantly associated with purchasing behavior. Conclusions: These findings provide field-based evidence suggesting that olfactory cues may be associated with a shift toward food choices perceived as healthier in vending-machine environments, pointing to their potential as a low-cost sensory nudging strategy while highlighting the need for confirmation through randomized or counterbalanced designs and replication across diverse real-world food-choice settings beyond university contexts.

paper.title: Neuroimaging insights into the effects of non-nutritive sweeteners on appetite regulation: A systematic review.
paper.abstract: Non-nutritive sweeteners (NNS) are increasingly used as low- or zero-calorie alternatives to sugar while maintaining sweetness. However, uncoupling sweet taste from caloric content may alter appetite regulation and promote food-seeking behavior, although the underlying neural mechanisms remain poorly understood. To address this, we conducted a systematic review in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched up to June 2025 using terms related to NNS, neuroimaging and appetite regulation. Of 137 screened records, 21 neuroimaging reports met predefined PICO-based eligibility criteria. Eligible reports included healthy adults across weight categories and examined artificial or naturally occurring NNS (e.g., sucralose, erythritol) compared with nutritive sweeteners (NS; e.g., sucrose) or non-sweet controls (e.g., water). Outcomes included appetite-related brain responses measured using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) or positron emission tomography (PET), as well as associations with gut hormones, glucose metabolism, and eating behavior. NNS and NS both engaged gustatory and reward-related brain regions, with some reports showing reduced activity and lower pleasantness ratings for NNS. Hypothalamic activity and functional connectivity were also modulated by NNS intake, with no observed associations between brain responses and gut hormones or glucose metabolism in the available reports. Overall, the evidence remains limited and varies by NNS type, dose, delivery method, habitual intake, sex, weight status, and metabolic state. Future studies should investigate acute and long-term NNS consumption under real-world conditions with greater ethnic and demographic diversity, accounting for individual variability to better inform dietary guidelines.

paper.title: Sweet Relief: Behaviorally conditioned analgesia in rats with inflammatory pain.
paper.abstract: The sensation of pain is modulated by a variety of physiological and psychological factors resulting in nocebo hyperalgesia and placebo analgesia. Modern pain therapy is increasingly regarded as a multimodal approach that combines pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions. Associative-learning paradigms offer a promising adjunctive strategy for improving pain relief. To elucidate the neurobiological underpinnings, translation into an animal model is therefore warranted. Here, we aimed to apply a taste-associative learning paradigm in a model of inflammatory pain to induce a state of conditioned analgesia in rats. Male Dark Agouti rats received an intraplantar injection of Complete Freund's adjuvant (CFA) to elicit inflammatory pain; ibuprofen (100 mg/kg) was used as analgesic. Pain-associated behavioral changes were assessed in an open field test, Von Frey test, and Plantar Heat test. For the conditioning experiments, treatment with ibuprofen as unconditioned stimulus (US) was paired to the presentation of a sweet taste of saccharin (conditioned stimulus; CS) on days 2, 4, and 6 after CFA-injection (acquisition). On day 8, conditioned responses were evoked by presenting saccharin followed by a placebo injection (retrieval). CFA induced clear behavioral adaptations, including reduced water intake, weight loss, diminished locomotor activity, and lower mechanical and thermal withdrawal thresholds. Spontaneous pain-associated behaviors returned to baseline from day 2 post-CFA, whereas stimulus-evoked behaviors remained attenuated throughout the experiment. Treatment with ibuprofen markedly raised withdrawal thresholds, confirming its analgesic effect. Pairing ibuprofen (US) with saccharin (CS) produced a conditioned taste avoidance (CTA). Rats that had undergone the conditioning displayed conditioned analgesia, evidenced by elevated thermal and mechanical withdrawal thresholds compared to the non-conditioned vehicle group. Our results demonstrate that a state of conditioned analgesia can be induced in rats using a taste-associative learning paradigm. Consequently, our model constitutes a valuable tool for further investigating the neurobiological mechanisms involved in placebo-mediated analgesia.

paper.title: Developmental stage determines the efficacy of silica nanoparticles in shaping maize defence, aphid performance and tritrophic interactions.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Silica nanoparticles (SiNPs) are emerging as promising elicitors of plant defence, yet how plant developmental stage influences their effectiveness remains poorly understood. We investigated whether maize vegetative stage modulates SiNP-mediated defence responses, and their consequences for herbivores and natural enemies. We hypothesized that SiNPs induce stage- and concentration-dependent defence, with stronger effects at earlier vegetative stages.

RESULTS: Maize plants at four vegetative stages (V3-V6; corresponding to stages 1-4) were treated with different SiNP concentrations, and responses were assessed across multiple biological levels. SiNP application did not significantly affect plant height, leaf length, root length or dry root weight across stages. However, leaf surface hydrophobicity and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) accumulation increased, whereas malondialdehyde (MDA) levels decreased, indicating enhanced oxidative defences and reduced lipid peroxidation. SiNP treatment significantly altered volatile organic compound (VOC) profiles, notably increasing levels of key compounds, such as sesquiterpenes. Aphid (Rhopalosiphum maidis) survival, fecundity and population growth were reduced on treated plants, accompanied by reduced settlement in choice assays, whereas olfactory preference in Y-tube tests remained unchanged. Foraging duration of the parasitoid Aphidius gifuensis increased on SiNP-treated plants at early stages, while predator (Harmonia axyridis) behaviour was unaffected.

CONCLUSION: Maize developmental stage critically determines the efficacy of SiNP-induced defence and its cascading effects across trophic levels. These findings provide mechanistic insights for optimizing the timing of SiNP application in sustainable integrated pest management strategies, enhancing plant resistance while supporting beneficial natural enemies. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.

paper.title: lickcalc: Easy Analysis of Lick Microstructure in Experiments of Rodent Ingestive Behaviour.
paper.abstract: Lick microstructure is a term used in behavioural neuroscience to describe the information that can be obtained from a detailed examination of rodent drinking behaviour. Rather than simply recording total intake (volume consumed), lick microstructure examines how licks are grouped and the spacing of these groups of licks. This type of analysis can provide important insights into why an animal is drinking, for example, whether it is influenced by taste or affected by the consequences of consumption (e.g., feeling 'full'). Here, we present a software package, lickcalc, that allows detailed microstructural analysis of licking patterns. The software is browser based and is hosted at https://lickcalc.uit.no, or the repository can be downloaded and installed locally. Lick timestamps can be loaded from a variety of formats, and different analysis and plotting options allow quality control of data and the determination of critical parameters for microstructural analysis, including the number and size of lick bursts. Data can be divided into epochs for detailed examination of changes across the session. Batch processing and custom configurations are supported. In this manuscript, we demonstrate the use of the functions exposed by lickcalc by analysing data comparing lick patterns between mice on a protein-restricted and a control (non-restricted) diet. We show that lickcalc allows quality control of the data and the uncovering of subtle differences in lick behaviour that are not apparent when just considering the total number of licks. This software makes microstructural analysis accessible to any researcher who wishes to employ it while providing sophisticated analyses with high scientific value.

paper.title: Morphological description of the oropharyngeal cavity of Kinosternon scorpioides scorpioides (Linnaeus, 1766), (Testudines: Kinosternidae).
paper.abstract: The oropharyngeal cavity of turtles exhibits considerable morphological diversity associated with differences in habitat, diet, and feeding strategies. However, the structural organization of this region remains poorly characterized in many Testudines, including Kinosternon scorpioides scorpioides, therefore, we aim to characterize the morphological aspects of the oropharyngeal cavity of K. s. scorpioides reported using macroscopic descriptions, light microscopy (LM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). LM revealed that almost the entire epithelium lining the oropharyngeal cavity of K. s. scorpioides is of the non-keratinized stratified mucous type, containing many mucous cells and numerous mucous glands throughout the lingual epithelium, palate and floor of the mouth, with the exception of the region located near the rhinopharynx, which presented a stratified keratinized squamous epithelial tissue containing taste buds, not observed on the tongue. SEM revealed that the entire epithelium of the oropharyngeal cavity has pores that are likely associated with the mucous glands observed in LM, and the surface of the tongue is covered by voluminous lingual papillae of varying sizes and shapes (filiform and fungiform types), which had cells covered by microvilli and/or microcysts. No salivary glands were observed. Compared with morphological data from other species, this study indicates that the epithelial structure of the oropharyngeal cavity of K. s. scorpioides is consistent with that observed in other generalist omnivores with semi-aquatic habits, thus corresponding to ecological information about this species.

paper.title: Characterization of Dopamine Receptors in Sepia officinalis (Cephalopoda): An Insight Into the Evolution of Dopamine Receptors in Bilateria.
paper.abstract: Dopamine is present in all metazoans but signaling pathways and receptors characteristics have been studied mainly in vertebrates. We addressed this issue by studying dopamine receptors in cephalopods (Sepia officinalis), a clade well-known for its visual and cognitive behavior and its production of various neurotransmitters. For the first time, we have phylogenetically identified three distinct families of dopamine receptors in Sepia embryos, belonging to the D1-like, D2-like and "invertebrate-type dopamine receptors" (INDR). We confirm that the family of INDR is not specific to Ecdysozoans and might have already been present in the ancestor of bilaterians and secondarily lost in Olfactores. Through cellular signaling assays we were able to functionally confirm the identification of Sepia dopamine receptors and show that they use three different signaling pathways. Finally we showed that all these three receptors were differentially expressed in the eyes and central nervous system of Sepia officinalis at the time of their setting-up. It is therefore likely that different dopamine receptors and different signaling pathways contribute to different physiological processes. This study opens the way to physiological and molecular studies on the organization and role of these dopaminergic system in cephalopods.

paper.title: Endosome-associated Rab GTPases control distinct aspects of neural circuit assembly.
paper.abstract: Neural circuit assembly relies on the precise regulation of cell-surface receptors that mediate signaling and adhesion. Endocytosis controls receptor activity and availability by internalizing and routing proteins through early endosomes to one of two main pathways: recycling back to the cell-surface or delivery to lysosomes for degradation. Rab GTPases direct receptors into these distinct pathways, but their specific contributions to circuit formation remain opaque. Using clonal analyses with null alleles, we dissected the roles of Rab-mediated trafficking to early, late, and recycling endosomes across multiple stages of circuit assembly in vivo. Our approach revealed that Rab5 and Rab11 regulate extensive and largely distinct developmental events, highlighting the pivotal roles of early endosome sorting and recycling pathways in circuit assembly. As neurons mature, both the spatial distribution and abundance of specific endocytic compartments change to reflect evolving trafficking demands. Our findings underscore how distinct post-endocytic trafficking fates are necessary to build neural circuits.

paper.title: Approval-standardized postmarketing safety reporting phenotypes of talquetamab versus BCMA-directed bispecific antibodies in multiple myeloma.
paper.abstract: Bispecific antibodies directed against B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA) or G protein-coupled receptor class C group 5 member D have partly distinct toxicity profiles, but unequal time since approval complicates postmarketing comparisons. Talquetamab was compared with pooled BCMA-directed reports across 12 prespecified toxicity domains using reporting-maturity×region-stratified Mantel-Haenszel (MH) odds ratios (ORs) with Holm correction. Among 3685 primary-suspect reports, talquetamab reporting was enriched for dysgeusia/taste disorder (MH OR 93.37, 95% CI 43.40-200.89), nail toxicity (72.21, 27.68-188.37), weight loss (10.53, 6.46-17.15), and skin toxicity (6.33, 4.83-8.29); infection was enriched among BCMA-directed reports (0.41, 0.33-0.50). Only one postapproval talquetamab report was available in that database, precluding direct assessment of the four talquetamab-enriched phenotypes. Approval-standardized FAERS reporting identified registration-recognized phenotypes that may inform toxicity surveillance and supportive care. These estimates describe reporting composition, not incidence, comparative risk, or causal effects.

paper.title: [Mechanism of total iridoids from Gardeniae Fructus in treating ulcerative colitis based on "bitterness drying dampness" theory].
paper.abstract: This study aimed to explore the mechanism of total iridoids from Gardeniae Fructus in treating ulcerative colitis(UC) in rats from the perspective of the " bitterness drying dampness" theory in TCM. SD rats were randomly divided into a blank group, a model group, groups of high-and low-dose total iridoids from Gardeniae Fructus(200 and 100 mg·kg~(-1), respectively), and a positive drug group, with 10 rats per group. Except for the blank group, UC model was induced in all other groups via enema administration of 2,4, 6-trinitrobenzene sulfonic acid(TNBS) solution(100 mg·kg~(-1)). During the administration period, the appearance of the rats was observed and recorded daily, and the disease activity index(DAI) was scored. Colon length and spleen weight were measured, and the colon mucosal damage index(CMDI) was scored. Microscopic pathological damage in the colon was observed via HE staining and AB staining, and the histopathological index(HI) was scored. The levels of inflammatory cytokines tumor necrosis factor-α(TNF-α), interleukin-6(IL-6), interleukin-10(IL-10), and 3',5'-cyclicade-nosine monophosphate(cAMP) in colon tissue were detected by ELISA. The expression levels and distribution/damage of intercellular tight junction proteins E-cadherin, claudin-1, and occludin in the colon mucosal layer were detected using Western blot and immunofluorescence. The expression levels of bitter taste receptor 38(TAS2R38), phospholipase C β2( PLCβ2), inositol 1,4,5-trisphos-phate( IP3), and α-gustducin(GNAT3) were detected by Western blot and RT-qPCR. The results showed that compared with the blank group, rats in the model group exhibited a significant decrease in body weight and a significant increase in DAI score. Furthermore, colon length was significantly shortened, while the spleen index, CMDI, and HI scores were all significantly increased. Concomitantly, the levels of TNF-α and IL-6 in colon tissue were significantly elevated, while IL-10 levels were significantly decreased. Additionally, the protein expression levels of E-cadherin, claudin-1, and occludin were significantly reduced. The protein expression level of TAS2R38 was significantly downregulated, and the protein and mRNA expression levels of PLCβ2, IP3, GNAT3 in colon tissue were significantly downregulated, and the content of cAMP was significant reduced. Administration of total iridoids from Gardeniae Fructus significantly improved all the above indicators in UC rats. These treatments significantly enhanced TAS2R38 protein expression in colonic tissues, restored the protein and mRNA expression of PLCβ2, IP3 and GNAT3, and raised cAMP content. In conclusion, total iridoids from Gardeniae Fructus may alleviate colonic epithelial barrier damage and inflammatory responses by activating TAS2R38 and regulating the GNAT3/cAMP and PLCβ2/IP3 signaling pathways, thereby improving symptoms in UC rats.

paper.title: Improved pork quality and pig performance through a circular feeding strategy: A sustainable approach.

paper.title: Untargeted salivary metabolomics for early prediction of chemotherapy-induced oral toxicities in patients with oral squamous cell carcinoma.
paper.abstract: Chemotherapy-induced oral toxicities, including oral mucositis, xerostomia, and dysgeusia, are common complications in patients with oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), often leading to impaired quality of life, treatment interruptions, and poor therapeutic outcomes. Reliable non-invasive biomarkers capable of predicting these toxicities before severe clinical manifestations remain limited. This study investigated salivary metabolomic alterations associated with chemotherapy-induced oral toxicities using untargeted liquid chromatography-quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometry (LC-QTOF-MS). A prospective observational study was conducted among 60 patients with histopathologically confirmed OSCC receiving platinum-based chemotherapy. Unstimulated saliva samples were collected before and after chemotherapy and analyzed using untargeted LC-QTOF-MS. Metabolomic data were processed using Agilent MassHunter software and annotated against HMDB, METLIN, LipidMaps, and KEGG databases. Principal component analysis (PCA), partial least squares-discriminant analysis (PLS-DA), variable importance in projection (VIP) analysis, hierarchical clustering, volcano plot analysis, KEGG pathway enrichment, multivariable logistic regression, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis were performed to identify biomarkers associated with chemotherapy-induced oral toxicities. Oral mucositis occurred in 63.3% of patients, xerostomia in 55.0%, dysgeusia in 48.3%, and severe mucositis in 18.3%. Untargeted metabolomic profiling identified significant perturbations in lipid metabolism, oxidative stress, and amino acid metabolism. Ceramide, lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC), glutathione disulfide, arachidonic acid, taurine, and citrulline were among the most significantly dysregulated metabolites. PCA and PLS-DA demonstrated distinct metabolic separation between patients with and without oral toxicity (R² = 0.86; Q² = 0.74; permutation p < 0.001). KEGG pathway analysis revealed significant enrichment of glycerophospholipid, sphingolipid, glutathione, arachidonic acid, arginine, and taurine metabolic pathways. Ceramide (adjusted OR = 4.82, 95% CI: 2.11-10.96), LPC (adjusted OR = 3.64, 95% CI: 1.78-7.52), and glutathione (adjusted OR = 2.92, 95% CI: 1.39-6.12) were independent predictors of severe oral toxicity. ROC analysis demonstrated strong discriminatory performance for ceramide (AUC = 0.91), LPC (AUC = 0.88), and glutathione (AUC = 0.85), while the combined metabolomic model achieved an AUC of 0.95, with 90.9% sensitivity and 91.2% specificity. Untargeted salivary LC-QTOF-MS metabolomics identified distinct metabolic signatures associated with chemotherapy-induced oral toxicities in patients with OSCC. Dysregulation of lipid metabolism, oxidative stress pathways, and amino acid metabolism appears to play a central role in the development of oral mucositis, xerostomia, and dysgeusia. Ceramide, lysophosphatidylcholine, and glutathione emerged as promising non-invasive biomarkers with strong discriminatory potential for identifying patients at increased risk of severe oral toxicity. These findings support the potential application of salivary metabolomics for early risk stratification, treatment monitoring, and personalized supportive care; however, external validation in larger, independent multicentre cohorts is required before clinical implementation.

paper.title: Supramolecular aggregate packing transitions as a strategy for molecular discrimination.
paper.abstract: Inspired by the conformational rearrangements of G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) during signal transduction in the human olfactory system, this study proposes and validates a molecular discrimination strategy based on packing mode transitions of organic supramolecular aggregates. This work validates the feasibility of using structural responses of supramolecular aggregates for molecular discrimination and offers new experimental and theoretical perspectives on the structural behavior of organic aggregates upon chemical perturbation.
